content: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbation is defined as an acute worsening of a patient’s baseline respiratory symptoms, such as dyspnea, cough, and/or sputum production, that exceeds normal day-to-day variations and necessitates a change in medication. Causes of COPD Exacerbation Life-Threatening Causes Life-threatening causes are conditions that, if left untreated, may result in death or permanent disability within 24 hours. These include: Arrhythmia Congestive heart failure Pleural effusion Pneumonia Pneumothorax Pulmonary embolism Common Causes Respiratory tract infections, which account for approximately half of cases. Unknown causes, which account for about one-third of cases. Exposure to air pollutants. Management of COPD Exacerbation Pharmacologic Treatment The presence of purulent sputum during an exacerbation is often sufficient to justify the initiation of empirical antibiotic therapy. Upon presentation to the emergency department (ED), the first steps include administering controlled oxygen therapy and assessing whether the exacerbation is life-threatening. If it is, the patient should be admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) immediately. Short-acting inhaled β2-agonists, with or without short-acting anticholinergics, are the preferred bronchodilators for managing exacerbations. A systematic review has shown no significant differences in FEV1 (forced expiratory volume in 1 second) between metered-dose inhalers (MDIs) and nebulizers, although nebulizers may be more convenient for sicker or frail patients. Intravenous methylxanthines (e.g., theophylline or aminophylline) should only be used in selected cases where there is insufficient response to short-acting bronchodilators. Systemic corticosteroids during exacerbations reduce recovery time, improve FEV1 and arterial oxygen tension (PaO2), and lower the risk of early relapse, treatment failure, and length of hospital stay. However, there is no consensus on the optimal dose or duration of corticosteroid therapy. The most common bacterial pathogens involved in exacerbations are Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Moraxella catarrhalis. Antibiotic selection should be guided by local bacterial resistance patterns. Empirical coverage for Pseudomonas aeruginosa is important in patients classified as GOLD 3 or GOLD 4. Procalcitonin levels may assist in determining the need for antibiotics. Maintaining an appropriate fluid balance is critical, with attention to diuretic use, anticoagulation, management of comorbidities, and nutritional support. Healthcare providers should strongly advocate for smoking cessation. After initiating oxygen therapy, arterial blood gases should be reassessed 30 to 60 minutes later to ensure adequate oxygenation without carbon dioxide retention or acidosis. Venturi masks provide more precise and controlled oxygen delivery compared to nasal prongs but may be less tolerated by patients. Noninvasive mechanical ventilation improves respiratory acidosis, reduces respiratory rate and breathlessness severity, and decreases complications such as ventilator-associated pneumonia, hospital stay duration, mortality, and intubation rates. Hospital Discharge and Follow-Up Before discharge, patients should begin long-acting bronchodilators, such as anticholinergics and/or β2-agonists, with or without inhaled corticosteroids. For patients who are hypoxemic during an exacerbation, arterial blood gases and/or pulse oximetry should be evaluated before discharge and within the following three months. If hypoxemia persists, long-term supplemental oxygen therapy may be necessary. Prevention of COPD Exacerbations Smoking cessation, influenza and pneumococcal vaccinations, proper inhaler technique, and treatment with long-acting inhaled bronchodilators (with or without inhaled corticosteroids) and phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitors are all effective in reducing the frequency of exacerbations and hospitalizations. Early outpatient pulmonary rehabilitation after hospitalization for an exacerbation is safe and leads to clinically significant improvements in exercise capacity and health status within three months. What Not to Do Assessment Spirometry is not recommended during an exacerbation because it is difficult to perform and the measurements are not sufficiently accurate. Treatment The use of mucolytics is not well-supported by evidence.
